extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Aristotelian ethics; readers of classical philosophy and moral theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explicating Aristotle's evaluative principles about happiness, virtue, moral responsibility, and intellectual/moral faculties as presented in a commentary/lecture-note style translation and notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness linked to virtuous action but requires a fair field
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness is identical with virtuous action only if that action is allowed a 'fair field' (i.e., adequate external conditions); otherwise they are not strictly identical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting happiness = virtuous action, understand this as conditional on having sufficient external goods/conditions; the commentary stresses the qualification rather than a strict unconditional identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness partly arises from human conduct (not purely a divine gift)
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness should not be thought of as a direct gift from Heaven independent of human conduct; supposing it comes at least partly from ourselves preserves motives for self-discipline and moral improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat happiness as partly endogenous to moral conduct; this view defends the value of moral effort and justifies striving for virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of innate incapacity for virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The commentator assumes it is not possible for a person to be born utterly incapable of virtue (what has been maimed was once perfect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral development presupposes some native capacity; moral education and habituation are meaningful because a capacity exists to be cultivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'Call no man happy till he is dead' (Solon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Solon's maxim can mean: (a) the man is happy when dead, or (b) the man when dead may be said to have been happy; distinctions include positive happiness vs. mere freedom from unhappiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this triage to assess claims about lifetime vs retrospective judgments of happiness; the commentary prefers the nuanced (b) reading and examines implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness should be based on the most abiding cause
rubrics_metrics.description: People expect happiness to be abiding, but fortune is changeable; thus a good definition of happiness anchors it in the most continuous/abiding causes (e.g., stable virtues or contemplative activity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer definitions of happiness that rely on durable features of life (character, intellectual activity) rather than transient external goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculative intellect (theoria) as most continuous activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle regards the working of nous or pure intellect (theoria) as 'most continuous' and therefore especially fitting as a candidate for the activity constitutive of the best life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh contemplative activity's continuity when assessing its claim to be central to happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: External abilities are instruments; proportion to one's work matters
rubrics_metrics.description: External abilities (wealth, instruments) are instruments of action; happiness in worldly respects consists in having instruments proportionable to one's station and tasks, fit for use rather than ostentatious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess external goods by suitability and sufficiency for flourishing rather than by amount or splendor.

rubrics_metrics.name: The dead's exposure to goods via friends is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal fortunes reflected from friends can affect the dead, but due to reduced sensibility the residuum of joy or sorrow is very small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering posthumous goods/happiness, account for decreased reception and limited emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustive division of goods: in esse vs in posse
rubrics_metrics.description: Goods are divided into those in esse (in existence) and those in posse (faculties/potential). The latter are good only when rightly used (e.g., rhetoric, money).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish possession of capacities/faculties from their right exercise; evaluate goods both by existence and by proper use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between moral and intellectual excellences
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual excellences may be commended merely for possessing them, whereas moral excellences are praised only for exertion and use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral virtues by performance/exercise, not merely by possession or potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enkrates vs akrates and the law of habituation
rubrics_metrics.description: enkrates (self-controlled) has unruly appetites but reason keeps them under; akrates (lacking self-control) lets appetites prevail. By habit, the enkrates approximates to sophrosyne (self-mastery), while the akrates' reason's remonstrances fade into akolasia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess moral character development as a gradual habituation process: self-control improves toward mastery, lack of control devolves into confirmed vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper understanding of Greek phrase echein logon tinos (substitution of Reason's logos)
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase denotes substituting that person's logos for one's own: in self-control the irrational nature substitutes Reason's orders for its own impulses; contrast with 'having mathematical truths' meaning actual possession of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating moral states, distinguish between internalized rational guidance (acting by Reason's logos) and mere intellectual possession of truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue consists in due regulation of all parts of our nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is the correct regulation of passions and parts of our nature; passions have a proper office and should not be eradicated but cultivated and harmonized into virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the Stoic error of extirpating passions; aim to form habits that bring passions into proper relation with reason (analogy: tuning instruments to make music rather than silencing them).

rubrics_metrics.name: Habits formed by actions, not by repetition of 'pragmata' alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions (praxis) form habits; mere repetition of results (pragmata) does not. Praxis denotes the whole process from conception to performance whereas pragma is the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral formation by looking at the agent's active processes and choices, not only outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral responsibility chiefly lies in applying rules to particular details
rubrics_metrics.description: Our moral responsibility is principally in the application of rules to particular cases; no rule can be so framed that evasion is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess moral blameworthiness by how rules are applied in concrete situations; remain cautious about rigid rule formulations that ignore particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity (nature) is a precondition of virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature must supply the capacity for virtue; one cannot be virtuous without the requisite natural capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging moral agency, factor in the individual's natural capacity as enabling or limiting moral development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maturation of virtue involves diminishing pain
rubrics_metrics.description: In forming virtues like courage and self-mastery, pain is initially necessary; as habit matures, the pain diminishes and eventually ceases when perfection is reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider endurance of discomfort as part of virtue formation; evaluate how friction decreases as habits solidify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praxis vs pragma: moral quality depends on the process (praxis) as well as result
rubrics_metrics.description: Praxis (action-process) can be right even if the resulting pragma is wrong (e.g., acting under erroneous impressions may not be called right); conversely, a right pragma may arise from wrong praxis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral actions by examining intentions, deliberation, and processes, not solely by outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice arises from a sequence: wish → deliberation → decision → will
rubrics_metrics.description: The mental machinery of action: a wish (orexis) leads to deliberation about means to ends, then to decision and the will (proairesis) which moves the body; pure compulsion halts the sequence and negates choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing voluntariness, trace whether the full sequence occurred; absence of deliberation/decision indicates non-voluntary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance distinctions: particulars vs principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of particular facts affects the rightness of the pragma (result), but ignorance of principles (incapacity to discern principles) shows a perverted moral constitution (conscience impaired).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between excusing ignorance of facts and condemning deficient moral perception; evaluate agents accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation concerns means to ends; chosen alternative gains distinctive status
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberation considers alternatives as means to ends; once one alternative is chosen it acquires the character of being chosen (bouleuton proaireton) while remaining an object of deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess practical reasoning by how means-to-end reasoning shapes decisive choice and subsequent agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: True courage requires two conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: True courage requires (1) exact appreciation of danger and (2) a proper motive for resisting fear; spurious forms fail on one or both counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate acts of bravery by checking both situational judgment and motivating aim (honor, the right end).

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice requires capacity, action, and moral choice
rubrics_metrics.description: To make up the character of Justice, a person must have the capacity, perform the acts, and do them from moral choice (i.e., voluntarily and for the right reasons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess justice in agents by checking all three components; failure in any undermines justice as a virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injustice understood as violation of equality (to adikon violates to ison)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every unjust act embodies 'the unjust' which is a violation of 'the equal' and implies unequal distribution (a greater and a less share).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating actions for justice, analyze whether equality or proportion has been breached and which parties suffer gain or loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction as bridging observation to universal; quality depends on the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's induction proves a universal by appealing from particular observed instances; its validity depends entirely on the quality of the particular mind performing it—rapid induction is often subjective, a mark of genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate inductive inferences by considering the cognitive faculty (nous) performing them; treat inductive certainty as subjective and probabilistic rather than demonstrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction is not exhaustive examination but probable reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction does not consist in examining all instances; it bridges a gap and is a branch of probable reasoning, not simple repeated apprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging inductive claims, avoid expecting exhaustive enumeration; instead assess the reasonableness of generalization given the mind's capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind attains truth either for its own sake or for further ends via distinct faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind contemplates for its own sake (aplos → episteme, nous, sophia) or for something further (eneka tinos → phronesis for action, techne for production); different faculties correspond to different kinds of truth and aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify intellectual activities and evaluate them by their aim (contemplative truth vs practical/productive ends) and by the appropriate faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of habits: passive impressions weaken as active habits are strengthened
rubrics_metrics.description: By repetition, passive impressions are weakened and active habits strengthened; passions thereby diminish in disruptive power and can be brought into harmony with reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess moral progress by observing diminishing disruptive impressions and strengthened habitual responses aligned with reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral assessment must consider social/political context vs individual character
rubrics_metrics.description: A person may be a good citizen (fulfilling social/political duties) while lacking perfection of individual character if the polity itself is faulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish evaluations of civic virtue from private moral perfection; context (the polity) affects what suffices for being a 'good citizen.'
